answer.exemplar: Diluting concentrated acid releases heat, and when the acid is the small volume the water is a large excess that absorbs it: adding 5.00 mL of 6.00 mol/L acid, which holds 0.0300 mol, to a large water volume keeps the temperature rise small and the final volume controlled. Reversed, a small amount of water meets 6.00 mol/L acid, the local temperature spikes, and part of the liquid can boil and spatter acid out of the vessel. The safety rule and the accuracy rule are the same rule, because a spattered solution also lands at an unknown concentration.

questions.explanation: The heat of dilution is large for a strong concentrated acid, and the amount of water present decides whether that heat is spread out or concentrated. Adding 0.0300 mol of acid to roughly 295 mL of water keeps the rise near a degree or two, whereas dumping that same 5.00 mL of 6.00 mol/L acid into 5.00 mL of water leaves an acid-rich mixture that can boil, which is why the rule exists. Note the arithmetic also fixes the dilution: 0.0300 mol / 0.300 L = 0.100 mol/L, so the final volume must be 300 mL if the final molarity is to hit the target.
questions.hint: Think about which material is in excess to absorb the heat of dilution.
